claims.text: The starting material is an untreated W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
A W/Cu-based joint is relevant to joining tungsten plasma-facing material to a copper-based heat sink in a fusion reactor.
Fusion-facing joints can experience high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy neutron flux.
Service exposure up to approximately 1200 °C is characteristic of the relevant W/Cu-based fusion-reactor joint.
An interlayer is needed between tungsten and a copper-based heat sink because their useful operating-temperature ranges differ.
Tungsten ligaments can be coated by a vacuum-based method such as magnetron sputtering before matrix consolidation or infiltration.
The proposed coating is a tens-of-nanometers-thick TiN or W2C layer deposited before Cu infiltration.
A TiN or W2C coating will remain a stable diffusion-barrier interface under high heat flux and irradiation.
The coating will prevent or substantially reduce W–Cu interdiffusion.
Reducing W–Cu interdiffusion will diminish phase separation.
Blocking exchange of W and Cu atoms across the interface will prevent local pore or void formation during thermal cycling and energetic-particle irradiation.
Coating-derived carbides can fill interfacial cracks and micro-holes and thereby improve composite density.
Interfacial pores and voids degrade effective thermal conductivity and structural integrity.
The coated W–Cu composite will have significantly lower W–Cu interfacial porosity than an otherwise identical uncoated composite after exposure.
The coated composite will retain higher effective thermal conductivity than the uncoated composite under fusion-relevant thermal and irradiation exposure.
The thermal-conductivity improvement may be approximately 10–20%.
The intervention is expected to be most effective in near-full-density composites with a uniform, well-controlled coating deposited before infiltration or consolidation.
Optimum coating thickness and composition may depend on irradiation level and temperature history, and coating delamination or cracking may limit performance.

Comparing identically processed coated and uncoated specimens after the same thermal cycling and simulated irradiation can test the proposed effect on interdiffusion, void density, and thermal conductivity.
